name: Colin Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself and how you came to line work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I built up a home security installation business over fourteen years, alarms, cameras, smart locks, eight vans at the peak. At 40 I sold it to a bigger company, put most of the money into investments and a rental unit, and decided I wanted to learn a real trade with my hands before I got too old. So at 41 I joined a private contractor that builds and maintains the big high-voltage transmission lines, the steel towers you see marching across the country. My wife Megan runs our home and the youth group at church, and we've got Ethan, who's thirteen, and Sophie, who's ten.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Transmission work is a different animal from street poles. We're climbing steel towers fifty metres up, replacing insulator strings and spacers, and sometimes a helicopter brings in the gear or helps pull the new wire. I'm still very much the junior, mostly on the ground rigging and sending up equipment, and Dale, our crew boss, only lets me up the tower on the simpler jobs with Arturo right beside me. I use AI every day, to study the procedures, to quiz myself on the tower drawings, and honestly to run the investment side of my life in the evenings. I love the scale of it and the view from up there. What wears me out is going from being the boss to being the slowest guy on the crew, and the long weeks away when we're on a job three hours from home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, the market spoke, and it turned out the tools were useful but not magic. I'd probably post something about how real work still needs real people. At work Arturo would give me a hard time about my phone quizzes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed, because I enjoy this stuff and I'd hoped for more. But for my family it's simple: I keep learning a good trade, our investments do what they do, and nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the apprenticeship and keep using AI to study faster. I'd keep the investments as they are. Maybe I'd look at whether there's a small business idea in line work down the road, once I'm qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AI Plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like a big game that ends nil-nil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sort of business idea in line work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small specialist crew doing inspection and repairs for the solar and wind farms, the private ones. Someone's got to maintain all those connections. I ran a business once, and I miss it more than I'd say at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wouldn't you say it at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Megan was relieved when I sold up. The business took a lot out of our family, long hours, stress. I promised her steadier years, and I mean to keep that promise, at least for a while.

S0.say: He'd say the market spoke and the tools were useful but not magic, and post that real work still needs real people. At work he'd take some ribbing about his phone quizzes.
S0.think: He'd be a little disappointed because he enjoys the technology, but for his family it's simple: he keeps learning a good trade and their investments carry on.
S0.do: Keeps going with the apprenticeship and uses AI to study faster. Leaves the investments as they are and quietly considers a small line-work business once qualified.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit flat, like a game ending nil-nil.
S0.quote: I ran a business once, and I miss it more than I'd say at home.
S0.fieldNote: Colin is a former business owner who misses running things and quietly keeps that from his wife. He sees the plateau through a market lens. He's comfortable with tech and a little disappointed it doesn't go further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how progress works: some jobs go, new ones come, and people who work hard and stay sharp do fine. I'd say the answer is apprenticeships and training, not handouts. At church I'd say families and community will carry people through better than any government scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think transmission work is in a good spot, because all those data centres need huge amounts of power moved across the country. And I'm the guy on the crew who's comfortable with drones, tablets and software. That's an advantage I'd use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dale to put me forward for any drone inspection or digital training the contractor runs. I'd study for my ticket even harder, so I'm qualified sooner. And I'd put some of our investment money into the companies building the grid, because I think that's where the growth is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing Steady Disruption?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. I like it when things move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew might struggle with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Arturo, maybe, though he's the best climber I've seen. He doesn't trust any of it. I'd help him if he asked, but I wouldn't push, a man has his pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said families and community will carry people better than government. What does that look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At our church, when someone loses a job, people bring meals, someone knows someone who's hiring, someone lends a car. I've seen it work. It doesn't replace a paycheque, but it's faster than any office.

S1.say: He'd say this is how progress works and that apprenticeships and training, not handouts, are the answer. At church he'd say families and community carry people better than government schemes.
S1.think: He thinks transmission work is in a good spot because data centres need power moved across the country, and being comfortable with drones and software gives him an edge on the crew.
S1.do: Asks to be put forward for drone inspection and digital training, and studies harder to qualify sooner. Moves some investment money into grid-building companies.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited by things moving.
S1.quote: It doesn't replace a paycheque, but it's faster than any office.
S1.fieldNote: Colin's outlook blends free-market confidence with real faith in church and community. He sees the grid boom as an opportunity and backs it with his money. He'd respect a sceptical colleague's pride rather than push him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough, and the people who move fast will be all right. I'd tell people to look after their families and their neighbours. I'd say the government should keep out of the way and let businesses create new work, though I'd admit two years doesn't leave much room for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy. My job as a junior would be gone within the two years, I've no doubt about that, but I've got investments and a business brain. What really worries me is my church, the men in our youth group's families, people without a cushion like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the crew within the year and set up a small company that leases the new line robots and runs them for the solar and wind farms, because someone will need to manage the machines on site. I'd move a chunk of our investments into robotics and power. And I'd use the business to hire a few guys from church, even if it's just to supervise the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a lot of nervous energy. It's how I felt the month before I opened my first business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having only two years change things, compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means you can't wait to be sure. In two years, whoever moves in the first six months gets the contracts, and everyone else is too late. I'd rather be early and wrong than late and right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you promised Megan steadier years. Starting a company in this picture isn't steady. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be a hard one. I'd tell her the steady option is gone either way, so it's a choice between risky and doing nothing. I think she'd come round, but she'd make me promise to be home for dinner, and I'd mean it.

S2.say: He'd say it will be rough and fast movers will be fine, and urge people to look after family and neighbours. He'd want government to let businesses create work, while admitting two years leaves little room.
S2.think: He'd be uneasy: his junior job would be gone within two years, but he has investments and a business brain. His real worry is church families without a cushion like his.
S2.do: Leaves the crew within the year to set up a small company leasing and running line robots for solar and wind farms. Moves part of the investments into robotics and power, and hires men from church to supervise the machines.
S2.feel: Uneasy with nervous energy, like the month before opening his first business.
S2.quote: I'd rather be early and wrong than late and right.
S2.fieldNote: Secure and adaptable, Colin sees fast AGI mainly as a business opening, though he worries about church families without savings. I named the clash with his promise to Megan, and he reframed it as risky versus doing nothing. He believes the first six months decide everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and anyone who doesn't use it has only themselves to blame. That sounds harsh, but I'd say it kindly. I'd push our church to set up a group that helps people plan and find training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is ideal for me. I can qualify, get real experience on the towers, and then start a business that runs robot crews, with the credibility of someone who's done the work. Customers trust a guy who's actually been up a tower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd qualify and get on every drone and new-kit trial. Around year two, I'd take a course in robotics maintenance and start talking to the solar and wind companies about what they'll need. By year four, I'd launch the business, using our investments as the starting money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Five years is enough to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone who doesn't use the time has only themselves to blame. What about someone like Arturo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. Arturo's 54, he's not a computer guy, and blaming him would be unfair, I suppose. I'd want to hire him, honestly, because the machines will still need someone who knows what a bad tower looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ethan about his future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be 18 by then. I'd tell him to learn something real, with his hands or with people, and to learn the technology too, so he can be the guy running the machines. And to keep his faith, because jobs come and go.

S3.say: He'd say five years is a fair warning and those who waste it have themselves to blame, said kindly. He'd push his church to set up a group helping people plan and find training.
S3.think: He thinks five years is ideal: qualify, gain real tower experience, then start a robot-crew business with the credibility of someone who's done the work.
S3.do: Qualifies in year one and joins every new-kit trial, takes a robotics maintenance course around year two, and launches the business by year four with the family's investments as starting money.
S3.feel: Calm, because five years is enough to do it properly.
S3.quote: Customers trust a guy who's actually been up a tower.
S3.fieldNote: When I pushed on the 'only themselves to blame' line using his colleague Arturo, Colin softened it and said he'd hire him. His plan is staged and credible. He mixes faith, family and entrepreneurship in one outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and there's no reason for anyone to be caught out. I'd say businesses and churches should lead, not governments. I'd be pretty upbeat about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is great for me. I'd qualify, get very good, and then build something on the robot side by year six or seven, without rushing. I'd be 53 when it fully arrives, with a business that runs the machines rather than being run over by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify by year two and work the towers for a few years to really learn the job. I'd invest steadily in robotics and power and start the business around year six. And I'd help Ethan and Sophie choose studies that mix hands-on skills with technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that worries you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The country, more than me. Ten years is a long time for people to tell themselves it's not coming, and then a lot of people get hurt at once. I worry the families at church will be in that group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is ten years different for you from two, if you'd start a business either way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, I'm gambling. With ten, I'm building. It's the difference between opening a shop in a panic and planning one properly.

S4.say: He'd call ten years a long runway with no excuse for being caught out, say businesses and churches should lead rather than governments, and stay upbeat in public.
S4.think: He thinks ten years is great for him: qualify, get very good, and build something on the robot side by year six or seven, arriving at 53 with a business that runs the machines.
S4.do: Qualifies by year two and works the towers for a few years to learn the job properly. Invests steadily in robotics and power, starts the business around year six, and helps Ethan and Sophie choose studies mixing hands-on skills and technology.
S4.quote: With two, I'm gambling. With ten, I'm building.
S4.fieldNote: Colin is the rare lineworker who sees AGI mostly as opportunity. His worry is for his church community, who may tell themselves it isn't coming. The difference time makes for him is gambling versus building.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, not for me so much as for the families at church without a cushion. Two years is too fast for most people to do anything. What would help is companies and churches getting organised early, real training tied to real jobs, and people like me who can start businesses hiring locally instead of just buying more machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask whether people want to keep working even if they don't need the money. I would. A man needs to build something, and I'd go mad sitting around with investments ticking over.

headlineQuote: I promised her steadier years, and I mean to keep that promise, at least for a while.
portrait: Colin Lopez is a 43-year-old junior lineworker on a private high-voltage transmission crew, after fourteen years building and then selling a home security business. He uses AI daily, has a strong cushion from investments and a rental unit, and holds traditional views on faith, family and free markets. Calm in the plateau and steady change, he stays only uneasy even with AGI in two years, planning to leave his crew and start a company that runs line robots. With five or ten years he stages that plan carefully, moving from gambling to building. His main worry throughout is for church families without a cushion like his, and his promise to his wife Megan of steadier years.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, mainly for the families at his church without savings, since two years is too fast for most people to act.
whatWouldHelp: Companies and churches organising early, real training tied to real jobs, and new businesses hiring locally instead of only buying machines.
